title: Randomized metric distortion in social choice
area: Algorithmic game theory, mechanism design and fair division
formal: Determine the infimum D* of the universal worst-case metric distortion achievable by any randomized ordinal voting rule, when the rule sees every voter’s full ranking and minimizes expected total distance to voters. The infimum ranges over all rules for all finite positive numbers of voters and candidates, with the model and zero-cost convention below.
why: A defining limit on how much welfare can be recovered from ordinal preferences.
status_note: The latest checked preprint, dated 8 September 2026, states upper bound 2.13713 against a general lower bound of about 2.11264. The exact value remains unresolved. These fresh upper bounds were matched to the model but their proofs and computational certificates were not independently audited; no full-resolution claim was found through 11 September 2026. The 12 September 2026 edit adopts absolute 0.01 benchmark acceptance; the saved open-status evidence concerns the underlying exact question and does not independently certify openness at that tolerance.
review_note: Specified full rankings, consistent pseudometrics, arbitrary tie-breaking, unrestricted lotteries, expected social cost and the infimum over all finite elections. Updated the old numerical gap using September 2026 primary statements, while separating rule-family lower bounds and proof-audit limitations.

sentences: What is the smallest universal expected metric distortion achievable from full voter rankings?
The voting rule selects a lottery without seeing the distances that produced those rankings.
The former value-two conjecture is false, with a general lower bound around 2.11264.

upgraded_from.title: The optimal randomized metric distortion in social choice

definitions: An election E consists of disjoint finite labeled sets V of \(n\ge 1\) voters and C of \(m\ge 1\) candidates, and a strict total order ≻_v on C for each \(v\in V\). A consistent distance d is a pseudometric on \(V\cup C: d(x,x)=0, d(x,y)=d(y,x)\ge 0\), and \(d(x,z)\le d(x,y)+d(y,z)\) for all points, with a≻_v b implying \(d(v,a)\le d(v,b)\). Distinct named points may be colocated. Equal distances may be broken in any order in the reported ranking; the guarantee must hold for every consistent pair \((E,d)\). The social cost \(SC_{d}(a)=\sum_{v\in V} d(v,a)\), and \(\operatorname{OPT}_{d}=\min _{a}\in C SC_{d}(a)\). A randomized ordinal rule f assigns each election E a lottery \(p=f(E)\), where \(p_{a}\ge 0\) and \(\sum_{a} p_{a}=1\). Its expected cost is \(\sum_{a} p_{a} SC_{d}(a)\). The lottery depends only on n,m and the full rankings, not on d or additional distance queries. It may use arbitrary real probabilities and unbounded computation. No anonymity, neutrality, incentive-compatibility or tournament-only restriction is imposed. Define \(Dist(f)=\inf\){\(D\ge 1\): for every E and every consistent \(d, \sum_{a} f(E)_{a} SC_{d}(a)\le D\cdot \operatorname{OPT}_{d}\)}, taking \(\inf \varnothing =+\infty\). This inequality requires zero expected cost if \(\operatorname{OPT}_{d}=0\) and avoids dividing by zero. Set \(D*=\inf _{f} Dist(f)\), over single rule families defined on all finite elections. The expectation is over the selected candidate, while elections and consistent metrics are worst-case choices. Replacing total cost by average cost divides both sides by n and gives the same distortion.
answer_criterion: Supply a specified real number a and prove in Lean that |\(a- D*|\le 1/100\). The proof must certify both a lower and an upper bound for the unrestricted quantity in this card. Equivalently, certified bounds \(\ell\)\(\le u\) of width at most \(1/50\) qualify by taking \(a=(\ell +u)/2\). An exact value with proof of equality also qualifies. An unevaluated copy of the defining extremum, a one-sided improvement, or a numerical estimate without a proved error bound does not meet this criterion. The \(1/100\) tolerance is benchmark acceptance; it does not prove an associated exact threshold conjecture.

context_blocks.title: Rankings hide the size of a preference
context_blocks.text: Two voters rank candidates a and b in opposite orders. Put a at 0 and b at 2 on a line. If voter 1 is at 0 and voter 2 at 1, the total costs of a and b are 1 and 3; if voter 1 is at 1 and voter 2 at 2, they are 3 and 1. Both arrangements fit the same rankings when a distance tie is resolved in the reported direction. The rule therefore has to make one choice of lottery that works in both possible geometries.

context_blocks.title: What randomization changes
context_blocks.text: If the lottery selects a with probability p, its distortion in these two examples is respectively \(3- 2p\) and \(1+2p\). At least one is at least 2. Choosing each candidate with probability one half reaches 2 for this pair of examples, whereas a deterministic choice suffers factor 3 in one of them. This demonstrates why randomization can help, but it is only a small lower-bound example. It does not establish the optimum over all elections.

context_blocks.title: The old value-2 conjecture is false
context_blocks.text: Charikar and Ramakrishnan construct larger elections giving a universal randomized lower bound of approximately 2.11264. Consequently, the target is to identify the optimal value above two, not prove the former conjecture. The lower bound concerns all randomized rules that use rankings, with no restriction to a particular named procedure or to pairwise summaries.

context_blocks.title: Recent upper bounds leave a smaller gap
context_blocks.text: Frank’s August 2026 preprint gives an upper bound of 2.5. Shah’s revision of 6 September improves this to 2.1441; its first version had the weaker value 2.3282. The 8 September preprint of Cai and coauthors states an upper bound of 2.13713, leaving a gap of less than 0.025 above the reported general lower bound. These are recent theorem claims with checked model matches; this review has not independently verified their proofs or numerical certificates. They still leave an interval rather than an exact value.

context_blocks.title: Restricted rules answer different questions
context_blocks.text: A weighted tournament records how many voters prefer a to b for each pair. It need not preserve all the information in their complete rankings. The optimal factor 3 for randomized tournament rules therefore does not bound what full-ranking rules can achieve. Similarly, Shah’s lower bound of 2.136 concerns his random-size-stable-lottery family; it is not a new universal lower bound for every rule. The scope of both upper and lower bounds matters when comparing them with D*.

context_blocks.title: Why this constant matters
context_blocks.text: D* measures how much total distance can be lost solely because a decision rule knows the order of preferences but not their intensities. It makes no assumption that voters behave strategically, and it does not require a truthful mechanism. The mathematical guarantee is robust across every metric consistent with the ballots, rather than an average over a chosen model of elections.
